title: Authenticated is not authorized: gate privileged message families at one chokepoint
statement: The handshake proves who a peer is; message families with real power (remote job execution) get a second gate keyed on a local registry row (`owned_devices`), enforced in exactly one function.

title: Gate remote-app pairing on an explicit approval that mints an origin-bound, scoped, expiring key
statement: Nothing is minted from a pairing request without the user's click: the approval modal defaults scopes to exactly what was requested but lets the user narrow them, offers only bounded expiry options, warns visibly on a non-HTTPS origin, and arms the Approve button after a short delay so a stray double-tap can't grant remote access. The minted key is bound to the requesting origin and claimed once.

title: Encode 'needs human approval' as data on the capability, and enforce the rule with a registry-walking test
statement: Each capability carries requires_approval, and a unit test walks the whole registry asserting any slug that does not read as read-only (list_/get_/count_/...) carries the flag — adding a new write capability without gating fails CI instead of surfacing in a live audit months later. A reverse test flags read-only capabilities that gate needlessly; deliberate exceptions (a read gated for prompt-injection reasons) carry their rationale inline.

title: Declare a command's auth level as an attribute, not a guard call
statement: Hand-written guard calls at the top of every handler are easy to omit and easy to mis-name, and the audit name drifts from the registered command. Use an attribute macro that prepends the correct guard and derives the command name from the function identifier, encoding the level vocabulary so an unknown level or an impossible sync/async pairing is a compile error with a written explanation. Keep the level visible on the handler so review can read the privilege at a glance — and be honest that annotating only sensitive commands means coverage is a policy, not a proof.

title: Decide access in a pure function; keep persistence separate
statement: Delegated-access logic that reads grants from the database inline can only be tested with a database and can only be reviewed by tracing queries. Split it: one dependency-free module resolves the scope decision from grants plus an injected clock as plain data, and a second module owns persistence of grants and the access log. Any externally supplied owner identifier must pass through that decision before a per-owner query runs, and a regression sweep should assert it.

title: Fail open in dev and closed in production behind one predicate
statement: Keyless dev and demo builds need auth and metering to degrade gracefully, but the same missing configuration in production must be a hard failure rather than a free pass. Express the degradation as one predicate used on both sides, paired with startup assertions that throw when the production condition is met. The request-time gate and any user-facing indicator must read the same predicate, or the UI promises something the API does not honour.

title: Express route authorization as one composable fail-closed policy
statement: Hand-rolled per-route ownership checks diverge, and the divergence is where cross-tenant reads slip through. Replace them with a single authorization function taking a small policy object, where opting into a cross-tenant fallback is an explicit flag that fails closed when its configuration is unset. Never gate that fallback on a demo or presentation flag — conflating a UI unlock with an authorization predicate is the classic fail-open, data-egress bug.

title: Enumerate expensive scopes per resource and time-box by default
statement: Issued API keys drift toward one blanket capability because enumerating targets is friction at creation time — and that blanket capability is what an exfiltrated key monetizes. Split capabilities into cheap toggles and expensive ones that must be named per resource, and make enabling the expensive one without picking a target a blocking validation error so no path to a blanket grant exists. Offer a never-expiring option if you must, but default the expiry to a finite window, and apply the mirror rule to inbound pairing requests.

title: Let a credential narrow a token's scope, and ship warn-before-block
statement: A third-party token usually grants far more than the user wants an agent to touch, and the provider's consent screen is not a place you can add granularity. Model an explicit scope layer above it: the connector declares its pickable sub-resources as data, the user's picks are validated against that declaration at save time so unknown keys and selection-rule violations are rejected at the boundary, and a per-credential enforcement mode decides whether an out-of-scope call is logged or refused. Ship warn-first so you can see what would break before you break it.

title: Treat an auth-provider flip as a session drain, not a config toggle
statement: When an app supports two auth backends behind one active-provider switch, the session reader only understands the currently selected medium — so flipping the switch makes every live session of the other medium invisible at once, with no error and no log to correlate. That is a silent mass logout, and it will be reported as an outage. If the risk is accepted, write it down at the switch and treat any production provider change as a planned drain of existing sessions.

title: Make tenant scope structurally unforgettable, not per-call discipline
statement: Every multi-tenant system fails the same way: one new query that forgets the filter. Put isolation in a seam that cannot be skipped — a database-enforced policy, or a scope argument the type system requires as the first parameter of every domain function — so a new query or route cannot silently produce a cross-tenant read. Per-route authorization functions and manually threaded tenant identifiers should be the documented exception, not the default; this portfolio already contains a case where the weaker form leaked.

title: Make the database enforce tenancy by demoting the app's role
statement: Row-level policies do nothing if the application connects as an owner or superuser, because those roles bypass them by design. Demote every pooled connection to a non-owner role at connect time so policies structurally apply to all runtime queries, and set the tenant scope as transaction-local configuration inside a scoped transaction so it can never leak onto a pooled connection reused by another request. Any wider read path (a pipeline worker) should be a separate, named, documented escape hatch — never the default.

title: Name every table that sits outside your RLS boundary
statement: A codebase that enforces tenancy through scoped transactions for its core tables usually also has an operational set — job queues, tokens, projects, onboarding requests — reached through the raw pool with the tenant identifier threaded by hand. That split can be deliberate, but describing the raw path as 'non-tenant' when genuinely org-scoped data flows through it misleads the next maintainer into trusting a boundary that is not there. Document the exceptions by name, or move them inside the boundary.

title: Resolve the tenant once at the request boundary and thread it down
statement: Multi-tenancy retrofitted onto a single-user schema usually means rewriting every query; making the organization identifier the owner's own user identifier avoids that entirely, since already-scoped queries are shared by construction. Resolve the active tenant once per request at the framework boundary from the session plus a cookie validated against the caller's membership set, then thread the value down into storage code that stays session-agnostic and unit-testable. Ignore a forged cookie, and fail fast rather than silently falling back to a shared default org.

title: Encode auth-flow invariants in the wrapper docs beside each call
statement: Pairing, CLI-capture, and gateway flows write their invariants into the wrapper docs beside the calls: origin-bound scoped expiring keys, scopes as a possibly-narrowed granted set, a server-authoritative expiry ladder, CLI capture decomposed into six separately-invocable steps each with its own result struct so the UI can render a wizard, results carrying token TTLs for refresh scheduling, idempotency on a DB UNIQUE with its routing consequence documented, and a warn|block enforcement dial with rollout doctrine written down.

title: On a 401 from an OAuth-backed call, force one refresh-and-retry — and drop your lock first
statement: A locally 'valid' access token can still be rejected (server-side revocation, clock skew), and the normal resolve path trusts local expiry so it will never refresh. Do exactly one forced token exchange + retry; release the per-credential refresh lock before calling the refresh helper (it re-acquires the same lock), and make force=true also evict the cached token or the retry re-uses the stale one.

title: When the provider has already burned the old token, retry the local commit until it sticks
statement: The moment a provider returns a rotated refresh token, the old one is dead — a transient local persistence failure (keyring lock, seal hiccup, full WAL) must not drop the new token or the credential is permanently bricked with no auto-recovery. Retry the commit with backoff and verify the write with a round-trip read inside the same transaction.

title: Clamp caller-supplied lifetimes into a server-owned window with max, default and floor
statement: Short-livedness is a security property, not a suggestion: the mint path clamps requested TTLs to a hard cap, applies a sane default when unspecified, and enforces a non-zero floor so a mistyped 0 doesn't mint an instantly-dead handle. Absolute expiry is stamped server-side, never trusted from the client clock.

title: Validate the system clock before minting anything time-bound
statement: If SystemTime::now() predates the epoch, timestamp helpers silently fabricate 0 and every freshness check downstream fails with a misleading symptom (e.g. 'Authorization took too long'). Check clock sanity once at mint time and fail with the real cause.

title: Consume short-lived tokens for the whole batch before any interactive pause
statement: When a batch operation redeems a one-time credential/session ref per item, create all items first and only then run the interactive follow-ups — blocking on a user prompt between creates can let the short-grace-window ref expire mid-batch.

title: Surface probably-forgotten API keys with a two-window staleness heuristic
statement: Flag an active key as stale when it is older than a creation grace window AND either never used or unused beyond an inactivity window — surfacing forgotten keys as an amber chip with a tooltip, not an auto-revoke. Keep both thresholds as named module constants so the knob is one obvious edit.

title: Store API keys as hashes with a display prefix, and separate audit-preserving revoke from delete
statement: The plaintext token leaves the backend exactly once at creation (behind an 'I have stored it' acknowledgment); at rest only the SHA-256 lives in the row, with a short key_prefix column for UI recognition. Revoke flips a flag so the audit trail survives; delete removes the row — two distinct actions with distinct affordances. The app's own internal system key is hidden from the user-facing list entirely.

title: Order auth resolution portable-first: a stored credential always beats local CLI auth, which is only a fallback
statement: When a capability can be satisfied either by a stored credential or by the vendor CLI's local login session, the stored credential must ALWAYS win when present — it is the only mode that survives leaving this machine (CI, another device, a headless run). The CLI probe is strictly a fallback for the no-credential case, because demanding a second hand-copied API token from users who already ran `vendor login` is friction they answer by skipping the integration entirely. Keep the probe off the hot path: memoise it in a TTL cache (long enough that one user action's many recomputes share a verdict, short enough that a fresh login is picked up) and bound every probe with a hard timeout since it runs on the UI's critical path.

title: Split bootstrap tokens from scoped managed tokens
statement: A service needs an operator break-glass credential that works before any database row exists, and it needs per-customer credentials that are scoped and revocable — conflating the two makes one of the requirements impossible. Resolve a bearer against a static environment map first with no I/O, then fall through to hashed managed tokens with per-token scopes and revocation. Define clearly what an unscoped bootstrap token means and which scope implies the others, so the check is one function rather than per-endpoint reasoning.

title: Keep the mintable scope vocabulary and enforcement in one place
statement: When scopes are enforced ad hoc per endpoint but must also appear in a central list to be mintable, the list becomes a second source of truth that drifts silently. An enforced scope missing from the vocabulary produces an endpoint that looks governed but is reachable only by an admin token — least privilege collapsed into all-or-nothing, discovered when onboarding a real customer. Mint through the real endpoint in tests, not through the store function, or the validation gap ships.

title: Size the auth model to the operator count, and say when it's unset
statement: A single-operator console does not need accounts and sessions; a shared secret compared at the one write path is the simplest correct choice, and pretending otherwise adds a surface to maintain and to get wrong. What matters is honesty about configuration: return an explicit not-configured result distinct from unauthorized, so the UI renders a real read-only state instead of a write path that cannot work. Validate enumerated inputs at the boundary too, since types are erased there.

title: Sign the OAuth state and report stale states as expired, not invalid
statement: An OAuth state value that is only a random nonce cannot tell forgery from lateness, so every slow enterprise sign-in surfaces as a CSRF warning and users retry into the same wall. Mint the state as nonce, timestamp and a keyed signature under a per-install secret, validate what the browser echoed back with a constant-time compare first, then check freshness separately so an authentic-but-old state gets its own outcome. Keep the freshness window deliberately larger than the user-facing accept timeout, and memoize the secret so a transiently unavailable keyring cannot invalidate live flows.

title: Keep the loopback OAuth listener alive past the first stray hit
statement: The redirect port of a desktop loopback flow is discoverable, so accepting once and acting on whatever arrives lets a port scanner, a stale tab or a forged request consume the consent — and the user sees a timeout. Loop instead: answer stray hits with the failure page, count them against a bounded budget, bound each accept by the time remaining against an absolute deadline, and stop on the first callback bearing an authentic this-session state. The absolute deadline is what stops junk traffic from extending the wait.

title: Serialize OAuth refresh per credential and persist rotated tokens
statement: Several code paths will eventually refresh the same credential at once — a proactive timer, a healthcheck, a manual rotate — and if two read the same refresh token and both exchange it, a provider that rotates refresh tokens invalidates the first exchange and the credential is permanently dead. Hold a per-credential async lock around the whole read, exchange and write sequence. Make the rotated refresh token a first-class field of the exchange result and always persist it, with a targeted write that cannot clobber concurrent field updates.

title: Parse expires_in leniently and seed an expiry at connect time
statement: Two independent bugs produce the same daily-401 symptom: a token that dies before the refresher expects it. Some providers return the lifetime as a JSON string, so a strict numeric read discards it and a default lifetime gets stamped that outlives the real one — parse numeric first, then string. And a fresh connect saves the refresh token but no live expiry, so a staleness guard skips the credential entirely; stamp a current expiry the moment a credential is connected or reconnected.
